classification.reason: The coach analyzes a match clip of Coco Gauff to explain the misunderstanding between practice tennis and match tennis, showing how players must train for awkwardness and adaptability.

problem.title_as_question: Why does your forehand fall apart in matches despite feeling great in practice?
problem.definition: Players experience a severe drop in stroke quality during matches because their practice is built around executing clean, identical swings in predictable environments, leaving them unable to adapt when match conditions force awkward body positions and split-second decisions.
prerequisites: Ability to hit clean forehands during practice drills, lessons, or ball machine sessions
problem.target_player: Players whose strokes perform well in static practice or lessons but break down completely in competitive matches

symptoms.description: Player's stroke falls apart and fails to produce the expected quality during competitive matches.
Player shanks the ball when forced to lean over, leave their feet, or alter their follow-through.
Stroke mechanics break down when the ball position deviates or when required to make active shot selection decisions.

causes.statement: The player lacks the skill set to coordinate their body and produce quality shots out of restraining conditions like being off-balance or coping with wind.
Practice sessions rely on clean, predictable feeds from ball machines or static cooperative rallies rather than simulating chaotic, split-second match situations.
The player operates under the false belief that athletic excellence comes from repeating an identical stroke pattern rather than achieving consistent outcomes through adaptable strokes.

angles.summary: The coach analyzes Coco Gauff contorting her body and hitting off-balance in windy conditions to demonstrate that awkwardness in matches is a display of elite skill.
True skill is not hitting the same stroke 100 times in a row, but producing the desired result using a hundred different variations under restraining conditions.
Match tennis feels like each shot is a unique car crash where players have milliseconds to decide how to coordinate their body.
Two players can look equally phenomenal hitting 100 crosscourt balls in practice, but the one who can play awkwardly in the wind will dominate 6-0, 6-0.
Training should build instincts and a set of sensations to react from rather than trying to execute a rigid, pre-planned swing.

solutions.summary: Make practice awkward by pushing into difficult situations, altering shot selection on the fly, and hitting out of unideal ball locations to test and adapt mechanics under stress.
